newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - BP studying in depth Brazil opportunities.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - BP studying in depth Brazil opportunities.

text.p: British Petroleum Co Plc is carrying out an in depth analysis of the opportunities arising in the Brazilian state oil industry which is due to be deregulated in the near future.

Dietrich Liebert, BP group representative in Brazil, told Reuters in an interview Friday, the company had delayed a review of the Brazilian market scheduled for the end of the first half of this year for another four to five months to carry out a more in-depth analysis of Brazil's oil sector.

"BP has decided it wants a more profound analysis of the Brazilian market before carrying out its strategic review," he said. "Brazil promises to be a growing and strong market. It is a very interesting market."
He said BP's interest in Brazil was increasing because of the positive changes in the Brazilian economy.
BP is also studying a data package provided by Brazilian oil giant Petrobras on future exploration and production joint ventures.

Petrobras has identified 150 projects it would like to carry out in partnership with private companies once the Brazilian Congress has approved the petroleum bill, which regulates the opening of the oil sector to private capital.
The projects are mainly in exploration and production and are worth around $3 billion in investments over three years.
Liebert said BP had no specific investment plans for Brazil yet because the petroleum bill still had to be finalized.
"BP would most likely be interested in the sale of technology or in a deal in the petrochemical sector." Liebert said. "In exploration you never say never, but for now we have no plans in Brazil."

He said BP would probably get a better return on its money by expanding and investing in existing exploration projects in Colombia and Venezuela than by investing in oil exploration in Brazil where it had to start from scratch.
Liebert said BP shied away from the high costs of mainly deep-water oil exploration in Brazil and the restrictions involved in dealing with Petrobras as a state-owned company.

"In exploration there are more opportunities for smaller oil companies," he said. "For them it is interesting to enter into a joint venture with Petrobras because they could get their hands on data and the exploration risk would be small because Petrobras has done all the ground work."
He said BP was most likely to step up its presence in Brazil in two to three years time when the Brazilian oil sector was really freed up.
"We are looking for the freedom to act without privileges being given to one party or another," he said.

The petroleum bill, which has already been approved by the lower house of Congress and is currently on its way through the Senate, is expected to pass into law at the earliest by the end of August and the latest by the end of November.
